profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This CyrusOne cluster spans Norwalk and Fairfield County, Connecticut and Wappingers Falls, New York. Wikipedia coverage of CyrusOne states the company acquired Cervalis, a Connecticut area data center and colocation provider, in July 2015 for approximately 400 million dollars, which is the most likely origin of the CyrusOne presence in this Connecticut and Hudson Valley New York cluster, though this fetch did not individually confirm the Wappingers Falls building by name. CyrusOne was founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten and was taken private in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.

reading.body:
CyrusOne NYM5 publishes 4 MW of IT capacity across 168,000 square feet of technical space. At 10 kW per rack, a common colocation density for mixed enterprise workloads, 4 MW supports roughly 400 racks; at 40 kW per rack, a common AI training density, the same 4 MW supports only about 100 racks. The ratio of technical space to IT load, roughly 42 square feet per kilowatt, is wide by modern AI standards and suggests the building was sized for lower-density, enterprise-style deployments rather than accelerator-heavy compute.

The single published certification is SSAE 16 Type II, which qualifies the facility for tenants whose auditors require third-party attestation of operational controls over financial reporting environments. No Tier rating, no ISO 27001, and no PCI DSS certification is published, so claims beyond SSAE 16 scope cannot be made from available data.

Connecticut has five data center facilities mapped in this site's dataset, and NYM5 is the only one with a published megawatt figure, making it rank first by default with 100 percent of the state's published IT capacity on record. That figure reflects the limits of what operators have disclosed to this site, not the true size of Connecticut's data center market. At 4 MW, NYM5 is a small facility by national AI-infrastructure standards, and its published specifications do not position it as a primary site for large-scale AI training or inference at current GPU cluster densities.
